i.x: Leviticus enabled ancient Israel to live in relationship with a holy God. But now that Christ has come as our High Priest and ultimate sacrifice—thereby fulfilling many of the requirements outlined in Leviticus—what do laws governing ancient Israel’s system of worship, with its priests and animal sacrifices, have to do with us? Leviticus increases our understanding of God’s holiness. And God’s demand for those who know him remains the same: “I am the LORD your God. . . . You must be holy because I am holy” ([Lev 11:44-45](Lev.11.44-Lev.11.45); [1 Pet 1:15-16](1Pet.1.15-1Pet.1.16)).

Leviticus continues the account of redemption that began with the promises made to Abraham ([Gen 12](Gen.12.1-Gen.12.20), [15](Gen.15.1-Gen.15.21), [17](Gen.17.1-Gen.17.27)) and the liberation of the Israelites from bondage in Egypt ([Exod 1–15](Exod.1.1-Exod.15.27)). The setting of Leviticus is the foot of Mount Sinai. The Israelites had not yet wandered in the wilderness or entered the Promised Land of Canaan. God had already established his covenant with Israel, declaring the Israelites to be his special treasure, royal priesthood, and chosen people ([Exod 19:5-6](Exod.19.5-Exod.19.6)). The people of Israel had received the Ten Commandments ([Exod 20:1-17](Exod.20.1-Exod.20.17)), the plans for the Tabernacle ([Exod 25–27](Exod.25.1-Exod.27.21); [30:1-38](Exod.30.1-Exod.30.38)), and the institution of the priesthood ([Exod 28–29](Exod.28.1-Exod.29.46)). The Tabernacle had been completed and dedicated ([Exod 35–40](Exod.35.1-Exod.40.38)). Now, in Leviticus, God spoke to Moses about his own holy nature, providing instructions about worship and conduct appropriate for Israel as his covenant people.

The regulations in Leviticus deal primarily with the activities and responsibilities of the priestly tribe of Levi, especially the high priest (see [Exod 28](Exod.28.1-Exod.28.43); [Num 3:44–4:49](Num.3.44-Num.4.49)). It includes God’s instructions about the Tabernacle, the priesthood, sacrifices, holy days, and ceremonial purity. Three main concerns are evident throughout Leviticus: the holiness of God, what is appropriate in worshiping a holy God, and how Israel was to be holy in relation to God.

A proper relationship with God begins with knowing who God is and understanding his nature. Yet, finite human minds cannot fully comprehend God, the Eternal One. Worse, if left to our own intuition, we inevitably begin to worship idols rather than the true God. In Leviticus, God graciously reveals his holiness in tangible ways and instructs his people how to worship him acceptably. Each sacrifice and holy day teaches the Israelites about God and what he requires of them.

God calls Israel to know him and to love him (see [Deut 6:5](Deut.6.5); [11:1](Deut.11.1)). As a result, they will also love and serve one another ([19:18](Lev.19.18), [33-34](Lev.19.33-Lev.19.34)). The rituals and regulations revealed in Leviticus teach the Israelites how to integrate love and service into their lives, both as individuals and as a nation.

Some scholars believe that Leviticus was written during Israel’s exile in Babylon (about 586–539 BC), long after the time of Moses. This view, however, does not explain why Judaism during the Exile, which was increasingly oriented around the rabbi and the synagogue, would be concerned with the priesthood and the Tabernacle. Nor does it account for Israelite worship prior to the Exile, aside from the liturgy contained or implied in the Psalms.

It is likely that Moses wrote Leviticus during Israel’s time in the wilderness after the Exodus. Both Jewish tradition and the early Christian church identified Moses as the author of Leviticus. Moses, raised in the court of Egypt’s king, would have been skilled in reading, writing, and mathematics (see [Acts 7:20-22](Acts.7.20-Acts.7.22)) and quite capable of writing Leviticus. The book begins and ends with statements affirming that the contents of Leviticus were given to Israel by God through Moses ([1:1-2](Lev.1.1-Lev.1.2); [27:34](Lev.27.34)). Leviticus repeatedly describes how Moses received the Lord’s instructions (e.g., [4:1](Lev.4.1); [5:14](Lev.5.14); [6:1](Lev.6.1), [8](Lev.6.8), [19](Lev.6.19), [24](Lev.6.24); [7:22](Lev.7.22), [28](Lev.7.28); [8:1](Lev.8.1)) and carried them out ([8:4–10:20](Lev.8.4-Lev.10.20)). The Old Testament often refers to Moses as the author of the Pentateuch (Genesis—Deuteronomy; see [Josh 8:31-32](Josh.8.31-Josh.8.32); [23:6](Josh.23.6); [1 Kgs 2:3](1Kgs.2.3); [2 Kgs 14:6](2Kgs.14.6); [23:25](2Kgs.23.25); [2 Chr 23:18](2Chr.23.18); [30:16](2Chr.30.16); [Ezra 3:2](Ezra.3.2); [7:6](Ezra.7.6); [Neh 8:1](Neh.8.1); [Dan 9:11-13](Dan.9.11-Dan.9.13)). The New Testament does the same ([Matt 19:7-8](Matt.19.7-Matt.19.8); [Luke 2:22](Luke.2.22); [24:44](Luke.24.44); [John 7:19](John.7.19), [23](John.7.23); [Rom 10:5](Rom.10.5); [1 Cor 9:9](1Cor.9.9); [Heb 10:28](Heb.10.28)). See also Genesis Book Introduction, “Authorship.”

Although it is set in an ancient time and culture, Leviticus communicates a timeless and vibrant message: God is holy, and he expects his people, whom he has rescued, to be holy like he is. God’s holiness and his gracious redemption provide both the foundation and the motivation for his people’s own holiness ([11:44-45](Lev.11.44-Lev.11.45)).

The priests stood between God and the people as mediators of the covenant. The priests interpreted what was holy and how holiness should be expressed in the community. The atoning sacrifices provided the way for the people to have their sins forgiven and to be made right with God (atonement). The non-atoning sacrifices celebrated the people’s relationship with God through gifts and shared meals. While surrounding nations offered sacrifices to their gods to appease them and gain their favor, Israel’s worship was not designed to manipulate God. Rather, the worship prepared and purified the people so that they could approach God. Each of the laws, ceremonies, and holy days teaches that God is holy and that he expects his people to be holy ([Lev 11:44-45](Lev.11.44-Lev.11.45); [19:2](Lev.19.2); see [1 Cor 3:17](1Cor.3.17); [1 Pet 1:15](1Pet.1.15)).

Forgiveness of sin and reconciliation to God directly relate to how people treat one another. Concern for social justice pervades Leviticus, which sets forth obligations to one’s neighbor, to the poor, and to foreigners. God expects those in covenant with him to love each other as an expression of his love (cp. [Matt 22:39](Matt.22.39); [Mark 12:31](Mark.12.31); [Luke 10:27](Luke.10.27); [Rom 13:9](Rom.13.9); [Gal 5:14](Gal.5.14); [Jas 2:8](Jas.2.8)).

b.x: The first major section of Leviticus deals with the institution of the sacrificial system and the priesthood. The sacrifices were either for atonement (the whole burnt offering, sin offering, and guilt offering) or for worship (grain offering and peace offering). Each one taught theology through a hands-on approach. Priests were required to officiate in the sacrificial worship at the Tabernacle, to instruct God’s people in the revelation given to Moses at Sinai, and to represent the people before God, such as on the Day of Atonement (ch [16](Lev.16.1-Lev.16.34)). Priests were provided for by receiving a portion of the offerings.

**The** **LORD called to Moses from the Tabernacle:** Leviticus is part of the ongoing narrative of the Pentateuch ([Gen 1:1](Gen.1.1)—[Deut 34:12](Deut.34.12)). It is part of the history of God’s saving acts: God chose Israel to be his people, delivered them from slavery in Egypt, entered into a covenant relationship with them, and guided them through the desert to the Promised Land. Specifically, Leviticus picks up with events recorded in [Exod 40:34-38](Exod.40.34-Exod.40.38), when construction of the Tabernacle is completed. It has been dedicated, and the Lord has filled it with his glory. Now the Lord gives Moses instructions for conducting worship at the Tabernacle.

The **Tabernacle** (literally *Tent of Meeting;* see study note on Exod 27:21) was an earthly representation of God’s palace. Inside the Most Holy Place, the Ark of the Covenant represented God’s throne ([Exod 40:1-33](Exod.40.1-Exod.40.33)). The Lord’s glory resided between the outstretched wings of the cherubim. There he would meet with Israel to communicate his will to them (see [Exod 25:22](Exod.25.22)).

**When:** This word introduces a major category (the process of presenting an offering), followed by a series of conditions introduced by **if** ([1:3](Lev.1.3), [10](Lev.1.10), [14](Lev.1.14)). This *when/if* pattern is generally followed through all the major offerings described in [1:2–6:7](Lev.1.2-Lev.6.7).
**offering** (Hebrew *qorban;* see study note on Mark 7:11) is a general term referring to all kinds of offerings and gifts, including the various offerings described in [Lev 1–7](Lev.1.1-Lev.7.38).

**burnt offering** (Hebrew *‘olah,* “what goes up”): The Hebrew word implies the ascent of **the animal** in flame and smoke. Except for its hide, given in payment to the officiating priest ([7:8](Lev.7.8)), this offering was burned completely on the altar ([1:9](Lev.1.9)). Its purpose was to satisfy God’s wrath against sin, ceremonially cleansing the worshiper and restoring him or her to fellowship with God (cp. [Rom 3:25](Rom.3.25); [8:3](Rom.8.3); [2 Cor 5:18-21](2Cor.5.18-2Cor.5.21)). The whole burnt offering occurs first in this list of offerings ([Lev 1–7](Lev.1.1-Lev.7.38)), providing a pattern for offerings that follow. It is the most common and most general atoning offering.

**male with no defects:** God allowed female and slightly deformed animals for certain types of non-atoning offerings (see [3:1](Lev.3.1); [4:27-31](Lev.4.27-Lev.4.31); [22:23](Lev.22.23)), but not for the whole burnt offering. In the dry, brush-encrusted hills of southern Palestine, cattle were much more difficult to raise than sheep or goats. This meant a bull without defect was an animal of great value. Centuries later, the prophet Malachi confronted the people for offering sick and lame animals instead of those without defect ([Mal 1:6-14](Mal.1.6-Mal.1.14)).

**Lay your hand on the animal’s head:** The sacrificial animal represented the worshiper in the ceremony ([4:4](Lev.4.4), [15](Lev.4.15), [24](Lev.4.24), [29](Lev.4.29), [33](Lev.4.33); [16:21](Lev.16.21)). This act signified that the animal’s death represented the death of its owner. In the ritual for the Day of Atonement, it signified that the sins of the owner were transferred to the animal ([16:20-22](Lev.16.20-Lev.16.22)). With the peace offering ([3:2](Lev.3.2), [8](Lev.3.8), [13](Lev.3.13)), the act seems to have indicated ownership of the animal being sacrificed.
The phrase **in your place** may mean “in payment for sin” (sometimes called *expiation*) or “as a substitute for the sinner’s death” (sometimes called *propitiation*).

**to purify you, making you right with him** (or *to make atonement for you*): Although older commentaries describe this process as “covering over” sin, recent scholarship defines it as “blotting out, erasing, or cleansing from” sin. The concept involves satisfying God’s wrath against sin, ceremonially cleansing the worshiper, and restoring fellowship with God in the community of God’s people.

**Aaron’s sons:** The descendants of Levi, Moses’ own tribe, were divided into two categories: (1) priests, who were descendants of Aaron, the first high priest; and (2) Levites, who served in subordinate roles ([Exod 28:1-4](Exod.28.1-Exod.28.4); [Num 18:1-7](Num.18.1-Num.18.7)). The instructions given here applied to later generations as well.

The **blood** was a symbol of life, not of death. The Israelite system of sacrifice was based on the principle of substitution, and the shedding of sacrificial blood was essential for atonement. It represented sacrificing the life of the animal as a substitute for the life of the worshiper ([Lev 17:10-14](Lev.17.10-Lev.17.14); [Heb 9:22](Heb.9.22)). The blood of Jesus Christ was shed as the ultimate sacrifice for sin ([Heb 9:11-14](Heb.9.11-Heb.9.14)).
The **altar** of burnt offering was located in the east end of the courtyard, outside the Tabernacle but inside the entrance to the courtyard ([Exod 40:6](Exod.40.6), [29](Exod.40.29)).
The entire animal was to be burned, except for the **skin***,* which was the priest’s share of the offering ([7:8](Lev.7.8)).

The Hebrew word translated **fat** describes the suet, or hard fat, from around the kidneys and loins. This specific term occurs only here and in [1:12](Lev.1.12) and [8:20](Lev.8.20). All fat—not just this special fat—was considered God’s portion ([3:14-17](Lev.3.14-Lev.3.17); [7:23-25](Lev.7.23-Lev.7.25); see [1 Sam 2:15-17](1Sam.2.15-1Sam.2.17)). Only the whole burnt offering was entirely consumed on the altar. With other offerings, the fatty portions and certain internal organs were burned; the rest belonged to the officiating priests and sometimes to the worshiper ([Lev 7:11-18](Lev.7.11-Lev.7.18)).

The offering was **washed with water** to remove dirt or debris that might contaminate the offering. Washing was also part of purification from ritual uncleanness, a prerequisite for Tabernacle service ([6:27](Lev.6.27); [11:28](Lev.11.28)).

**special gift:** The Hebrew term (*’isheh*) has traditionally been rendered “offering made by fire.” Although the offering was to be burned ([1:13](Lev.1.13), [17](Lev.1.17)), recent scholarship suggests that the word had the more generic meaning of “gift.”

**pleasing aroma to the** **LORD** (literally *a restful odor;* also in [1:13](Lev.1.13), [17](Lev.1.17)): Pagan people of the ancient Near East believed that their gods smelled the offerings because they needed to eat them to sustain their lives. Although God’s response is sometimes represented in language that reflects the cultural setting (e.g., [21:6](Lev.21.6); [Num 28:2](Num.28.2)), the Bible is clear that God did not need offerings as food ([Ps 50:9-13](Ps.50.9-Ps.50.13)). Instead, they pleased him as sincere offerings for the purpose of atonement.

Permission to offer lesser animals was to make the animal, and therefore atonement, more affordable to common Israelites. The method of offering these animals closely parallels the offering of bulls outlined in [1:3-9](Lev.1.3-Lev.1.9).

Birds were plentiful, cheap, and easy to catch. This meant that atonement and worship through sacrifices were not only for the rich and privileged; the poor were also included (see also [5:7](Lev.5.7); [12:8](Lev.12.8); see [Luke 2:24](Luke.2.24)).

**tear . . . without tearing it apart:** Cutting larger animals into pieces ([1:6](Lev.1.6), [12](Lev.1.12)) probably reflects the ancient rite of covenant-making, in which the participant passed between the two halves of a sacrificed animal (see [Gen 15:10](Gen.15.10)). Because of their small size, birds were not cut in half. If it was necessary to pass between them, they were arranged in pairs.

The **grain offering** (Hebrew *minkhah,* “gift, present”) was a way to express worship to the Lord through a gift, recognizing him as Lord over the life of the worshiper. The grain offering was to accompany each whole burnt offering ([Num 28:3-6](Num.28.3-Num.28.6), [12-13](Num.28.12-Num.28.13)), sin offering ([Num 6:14-15](Num.6.14-Num.6.15)), and peace offering ([Lev 9:4](Lev.9.4); [Num 6:17](Num.6.17)). The grain offering supplied the priest with bread for his daily sustenance, because no farmland was allocated to priests.
**Choice flour** was fine wheat flour (in contrast with common barley flour). See also [1 Kgs 4:22](1Kgs.4.22); [Ezek 16:13](Ezek.16.13), [19](Ezek.16.19).

Israelites used **olive oil** as shortening in their cooking, as lamp fuel, and for medicinal and cosmetic purposes. Accordingly, it was associated with the rich produce of the land and with God’s provision ([Deut 8:8](Deut.8.8)).

Like choice flour, **frankincense** was frequently connected with the Tabernacle ([Exod 30:34](Exod.30.34); [Lev 24:7](Lev.24.7)) or the Temple ([1 Chr 9:29](1Chr.9.29)). This fragrant tree resin was also used by individuals on special occasions ([Song 3:6](Song.3.6); [Matt 2:11](Matt.2.11)). It was a primary ingredient of the holy incense burned in the Holy Place as a tangible expression of worship ([Exod 30:34-38](Exod.30.34-Exod.30.38)).
The **representative portion** of the grain offering was burned on the altar to remind the worshiper that the whole offering belonged to God.

**rest of the grain offering:** A portion of the fire offerings was generally reserved for the priest as food (see [6:16-17](Lev.6.16-Lev.6.17)). Exceptions included the whole burnt offering (the priest received only the hide; see [7:8](Lev.7.8)), offerings given by the priest for himself ([4:3-12](Lev.4.3-Lev.4.12); [6:19-23](Lev.6.19-Lev.6.23)), or offerings made for the entire community ([4:13-21](Lev.4.13-Lev.4.21)). In these cases, the offering was to be entirely burned. The grain offering provided the priests with bread for their diet.

**most holy** (Hebrew *qodesh qodashim,* “holy of holies”): Both God and what belongs to him are holy. “Most holy” designates the priestly share as taken from the holy offering and reserved for a special function. This description is used for the priest’s share of any gifts dedicated to the Lord ([Num 18:8-10](Num.18.8-Num.18.10)).
A large ceramic **oven** was placed in a hole, and around it a fire was kindled. Once the oven was hot, the flat bread baked against the inside of its wall.
**without any yeast:** See study note on 2:11; see also [Exod 12:8](Exod.12.8).
A **griddle** was a flat stone or clay surface propped above a fire and heated. Later griddles were made of metal ([Ezek 4:3](Ezek.4.3)).
Dough **prepared in a pan** was fried with **oil** until crisp.

**yeast:** The bread commonly eaten in biblical times was comparable to modern sourdough. The substance that is often called “leaven” consisted of wild yeast spores mixed into moist dough or a flour mixture. The yeast would grow and cause the dough to ferment, souring and raising it. A reserved portion of the sour dough would be kneaded into subsequent batches ([Matt 13:33](Matt.13.33)). Unleavened bread was required for the Passover ([Exod 12:8](Exod.12.8)), in remembrance of Israel’s bondage in Egypt ([Deut 16:3](Deut.16.3)) and their speedy departure from that land ([Exod 12:34](Exod.12.34); [13:3](Exod.13.3)). Following the Exodus, unleavened bread acquired the status of altar bread. Leavened bread was not to be burned on the altar.

**honey:** The Hebrew word (*debash*) can also refer to fruit nectar. The reason for its exclusion is not stated, but perhaps the frequent use of honey in pagan offerings, particularly to gods of the underworld, was a contributing reason. If the word refers to fruit nectar, its association with wine and fermentation may have linked it with yeast, making it ineligible to be burned on the altar. However, both honey and yeast were allowed as part of an offering of first crops ([Lev 2:12](Lev.2.12)). Loaves of bread made with yeast were to be presented with thank offerings ([7:13](Lev.7.13)) and as a gift to the priest in the Festival of Harvest ([23:17](Lev.23.17)). In the New Testament, yeast becomes a spiritual metaphor, playing on its sour taste and on its tendency to spread ([Matt 16:6](Matt.16.6), [11](Matt.16.11), [12](Matt.16.12); [1 Cor 5:6-8](1Cor.5.6-1Cor.5.8); cp. [Matt 13:33](Matt.13.33)).

**offering of the first crops:** This offering (called “firstfruits” in many translations) was brought from the first part of the harvest ([23:15-21](Lev.23.15-Lev.23.21); [Num 28:26-31](Num.28.26-Num.28.31)). Like the representative portion of the grain offering, this offering acknowledged that the entire harvest belonged to God ([Lev 23:10-11](Lev.23.10-Lev.23.11); [Exod 22:29](Exod.22.29); [23:19](Exod.23.19); [34:26](Exod.34.26); [Num 15:18-20](Num.15.18-Num.15.20); [Deut 18:4-5](Deut.18.4-Deut.18.5); [26:1-2](Deut.26.1-Deut.26.2)). It further recognized that the land itself, not just its products, belonged to God; Israel was merely the tenant (see [Lev 25:23](Lev.25.23)).

In ancient times, **salt** represented permanence because it preserved food. A covenant of salt (see study notes on Num 18:19; 2 Chr 13:5) denoted an enduring covenant that was renewed with successive generations.

The **peace offering** (Hebrew *shelem*) expressed worship through fellowship with the Lord and with others. The Hebrew word is from the same root as *shalom,* which speaks of wholeness, well-being, harmony, and peace. *Shalom* means more than a cessation of hostilities between God and the worshiper; it implies a bond of harmonious fellowship. The peace offering was therefore a shared meal celebrating fellowship with God and others (cp. [Exod 18:12](Exod.18.12); [24:9-11](Exod.24.9-Exod.24.11); [1 Sam 9:15-24](1Sam.9.15-1Sam.9.24)). It could be presented as an expression of thanks ([Lev 7:12-15](Lev.7.12-Lev.7.15)), as a voluntary offering, or in fulfillment of a vow ([7:16-18](Lev.7.16-Lev.7.18); [22:21](Lev.22.21)). Peace offerings often followed whole burnt offerings (e.g., [1 Kgs 9:25](1Kgs.9.25)), showing that fellowship with God follows atonement. When we have experienced atonement through Christ, we are able to be at peace with God and with each other (see [Acts 2:42](Acts.2.42); [10:36](Acts.10.36); [Rom 5:1](Rom.5.1); [1 Cor 10:16](1Cor.10.16); [11:17-34](1Cor.11.17-1Cor.11.34); [2 Cor 5:18-21](2Cor.5.18-2Cor.5.21)).

**a male or a female:** The whole burnt offering allowed only the use of male animals because it made atonement ([1:3](Lev.1.3), [10](Lev.1.10)). The less formal peace offering permitted both male and female animals (see also [4:28](Lev.4.28), [32](Lev.4.32)).
**no defects:** The sacrificial animals had to be healthy. The only exception was the voluntary offering, for which a slight blemish was permissible ([22:23](Lev.22.23)).

**kidneys . . . lobe of the liver:** The Israelites saw the kidneys as organs of understanding, much like how we think of the brain (“I am overwhelmed \[literally *my kidneys are consumed*\],” [Job 19:27](Job.19.27); “heart,” [Pss 7:9](Ps.7.9); [16:7](Ps.16.7); [Jer 12:2](Jer.12.2); [Lam 3:13](Lam.3.13); “motives,” [Ps 26:2](Ps.26.2); [Jer 17:10](Jer.17.10); “thoughts,” [Jer 11:20](Jer.11.20); [20:12](Jer.20.12)). The liver represented life and vitality, similar to how we think of the heart ([Prov 7:23](Prov.7.23); “spirit,” [Lam 2:11](Lam.2.11)).

The **burnt offering** is described in [1:3-17](Lev.1.3-Lev.1.17) and is best referred to as the “whole burnt offering.” Because it was offered twice daily (see [Num 28:4](Num.28.4)), and because the need for atonement preceded fellowship, the text assumes that the burnt offering would be on the altar already. The priest was to lay the fatty portions and certain internal organs ([3:3-4](Lev.3.3-Lev.3.4)) of the peace offering on top of it.
**Sheep** were smaller, easier to raise, and less expensive than cattle. Apart from the exceptions mentioned in these verses, offerings of sheep followed the same pattern as those of cattle.
**broad tail:** Sheep in this part of the ancient Near East had broad, fatty tails that were burned on the altar with the rest of the fat.
**special gift:** See study note on 1:9.

Offerings of **food** were called “God’s food” ([21:6](Lev.21.6), [8](Lev.21.8), [17](Lev.21.17), [21](Lev.21.21), [22](Lev.21.22); [Num 28:2](Num.28.2)). However, Scripture is clear that the Lord did not eat the offerings, as pagans believed their deities did ([Ps 50:9-13](Ps.50.9-Ps.50.13)). Instead, these offerings belonged to God, and the priest ate a portion of this food as God’s representative ([Lev 21:21-22](Lev.21.21-Lev.21.22)). These offerings sustained the priest and his family.
The offering of goats followed a similar pattern as for cattle and sheep. Both goats and sheep were considered offerings from the flock (see [3:6](Lev.3.6)).
Human beings were not permitted to eat the **fat or blood** (see [1:5](Lev.1.5), [8](Lev.1.8) and study notes).

The **sin offering** (Hebrew *khatta’t,* from the root *khata’,* meaning “to lack, fall short, miss, fail”) was for specific unintentional violations of God’s commands (see also [Num 15:22-29](Num.15.22-Num.15.29)), intended to repair a loss or remedy a failure (e.g., [Lev 5:1-4](Lev.5.1-Lev.5.4)). Although we all sin, God will forgive us if we confess it ([Gal 6:1](Gal.6.1); [1 Jn 1:8-9](1John.1.8-1John.1.9)). But we are warned against sinning “brazenly” or “deliberately” ([Num 15:30-31](Num.15.30-Num.15.31); [Heb 6:4-6](Heb.6.4-Heb.6.6); [10:26-29](Heb.10.26-Heb.10.29)).

These verses distinguish two types of sin offerings: (1) the offering given for the sin of the **high priest** ([4:3](Lev.4.3), [20](Lev.4.20)) and **the entire Israelite community** ([4:13](Lev.4.13)), and (2) the offering given for **one of Israel’s leaders** ([4:22](Lev.4.22)) and **any of the common people** ([4:27](Lev.4.27)). The former case required offering a bull, a large, expensive animal. It was not to be eaten ([6:30](Lev.6.30)) but was completely burned ([4:12](Lev.4.12), [21](Lev.4.21)), and some of its blood was presented in the Holy Place ([4:6-7](Lev.4.6-Lev.4.7), [17-18](Lev.4.17-Lev.4.18)). The latter case required a lesser animal—a male goat for a lay leader or a female sheep or goat for a common person. The priest ate a portion of the layperson’s offering ([6:24-29](Lev.6.24-Lev.6.29)), and the blood was presented at the bronze altar in the courtyard ([4:25](Lev.4.25), [30](Lev.4.30)). The distinction stresses the responsibilities of leaders. The offering was the same for the priest as for the entire people, and the lay leader’s offering was more than that of a common person. The New Testament also emphasizes the responsibility of religious leaders; those who teach ([Jas 3:1](Jas.3.1)) and those who serve as religious leaders ([Matt 23:1-33](Matt.23.1-Matt.23.33); [Luke 20:47](Luke.20.47)) are judged more severely than those who follow them.

The **high priest** was designated by God and “anointed” (Hebrew *mashiakh,* “set apart by the ritual of anointing”) for a particular service. In [1 Sam 1:1—2 Kgs 25:30](1Sam.1.1-2Kgs.25.30), anointing most often refers to Israel’s king (see [1 Sam 24:6](1Sam.24.6); [2 Sam 1:14](2Sam.1.14); [19:21](2Sam.19.21)). While all priests were anointed ([Exod 40:13-15](Exod.40.13-Exod.40.15)), here the term probably refers to the high priest because he was specially anointed for service in the Tabernacle ([Lev 6:20](Lev.6.20); [8:12](Lev.8.12)). Since the high priest was mediator for all of Israel, including lesser priests, his sin would bring guilt on the entire assembly (see “Community Identity” Theme Note).
**Guilt** results from violating God’s will; it is not just perceived or psychological guilt (see study note on 5:17-19).

The **Tabernacle** complex had a tent (sometimes called the “Tent of Meeting”; see study note on 1:1) at the west end of the courtyard. Inside the tent, the **inner curtain** divided the first room, the Holy Place, from the second, the Most Holy Place. The Most Holy Place contained the Ark of the Covenant ([Exod 26:31-33](Exod.26.31-Exod.26.33)) and was God’s throne room (see study note on Lev 1:1). Sprinkling the animal’s **blood** before the curtain ([4:6](Lev.4.6), [17](Lev.4.17)) and applying it to the horns of the incense altar ([4:7](Lev.4.7), [18](Lev.4.18)) was done to atone for the anointed priest or for the entire congregation. This action demonstrated the gravity of the offenses being atoned for (cp. [4:25](Lev.4.25), [30-35](Lev.4.30-Lev.4.35)).

The **altar for fragrant incense** stood in front of the inner curtain, just outside the Most Holy Place ([4:6](Lev.4.6)). It had four protrusions resembling **horns,** as did the altar for burnt offerings (see study note on Exod 27:2). The priests burned incense on this altar to the Lord each morning and evening ([Exod 30:1-10](Exod.30.1-Exod.30.10)).

Only the offerings for the priest or the entire community were burned **outside the camp.** Perhaps this was commanded because the offering had figuratively absorbed the contamination of the high priest or the community and therefore had to be disposed of outside the camp. Those guilty were not to partake of or reap any benefit from their own sin offerings, even if they were priests ([6:19-23](Lev.6.19-Lev.6.23)).

The Hebrew term for **elders** is related to the word for beard. It implies mature but not necessarily elderly individuals. They were leaders of the community—typically, heads of families and tribes (cp. [Exod 18:21-26](Exod.18.21-Exod.18.26); [Deut 22:15-19](Deut.22.15-Deut.22.19)). For this offering, the elders represented the entire people, as they would later in anointing David as king ([2 Sam 5:3](2Sam.5.3)).

A similar form of the phrase **they will be forgiven** appears frequently in passages dealing with atonement ([4:26](Lev.4.26), [31](Lev.4.31), [35](Lev.4.35); [5:10](Lev.5.10), [13](Lev.5.13), [16](Lev.5.16), [18](Lev.5.18); [6:7](Lev.6.7); [19:22](Lev.19.22); [Num 15:25](Num.15.25), [26](Num.15.26), [28](Num.15.28)). God is willing to forgive a repentant person’s sin and restore him or her to the community of faith.

The sin offerings described in this passage atoned for laypersons, whether leaders or other Israelite citizens. These offerings could be eaten (contrast [4:3-21](Lev.4.3-Lev.4.21)), and they involved lesser animals. The blood of the offering was disposed of in the courtyard of the Tabernacle and not carried to the Holy Place. As with the peace offering (ch [3](Lev.3.1-Lev.3.17)), the fat and certain internal organs were burned on the altar. However, the rest of the meat from these offerings was given to the priest as food for himself and the males in his family ([6:29](Lev.6.29)), and it was to be eaten in a holy place ([6:26](Lev.6.26); cp. [10:16-20](Lev.10.16-Lev.10.20)). A lay leader was to offer a male goat ([4:23](Lev.4.23)), while a common layperson could offer a female goat or lamb. The animal’s lesser size and cost reflected the lesser influence of the common Israelite and, probably, their financial situation. Economic considerations allowed those who were poor to bring a pair of doves or young pigeons ([5:7-8](Lev.5.7-Lev.5.8); [12:6](Lev.12.6), [8](Lev.12.8); cp. [Luke 2:24](Luke.2.24)). The desperately poor could offer two quarts of flour ([Lev 5:11](Lev.5.11)).
**Israel’s leaders** included the elders (see [4:15](Lev.4.15)), tribal heads, and family heads (see [Num 1:16](Num.1.16), [44](Num.1.44); [1 Kgs 8:1](1Kgs.8.1)).

The **male goat** offered by a lay leader was a lesser offering than was required for the priest (a bull) but more than was required for a common person ([4:28](Lev.4.28), [32](Lev.4.32)). However, like all offerings used for securing atonement, the animal could have no **defects** (see [1:3](Lev.1.3)).
**at the place where burnt offerings are slaughtered:** See [1:3-5](Lev.1.3-Lev.1.5).

**blood . . . horns of the altar:** Unlike the blood of the bull for the priest, the blood of the offering of a leader ([4:25](Lev.4.25)) or a common Israelite ([4:30](Lev.4.30), [34](Lev.4.34)) was not to be carried into the Holy Place. Also, a portion of the meat was to be eaten by the priest who offered it ([6:24-29](Lev.6.24-Lev.6.29)).

The **common people,** who had less responsibility than a priest or leader, were permitted the lesser offering of a **female** sheep or goat. A greater position brings greater responsibility (cp. [Amos 3:2](Amos.3.2); [Matt 25:14-30](Matt.25.14-Matt.25.30); [Jas 3:1](Jas.3.1)).

These verses list examples of sins covered by the sin offering ([4:2](Lev.4.2)). When a person realized he or she had committed an offense, the next step was to make it right by admitting guilt and bringing a sin offering.
The first infraction was the failure **to testify** when called as a witness before a court. Failure to testify was not a passive act because it actively aided the criminal.

**you will be punished** (literally *you become guilty* or *you realize your guilt*): Anticipating God’s punishment for the sin, the guilty party offered the sacrifice to remove the guilt and escape the punishment.

**ceremonially unclean:** “Clean” and “unclean” did not pertain to hygiene (see [11:1–15:33](Lev.11.1-Lev.15.33)) but to suitability for participating in worship or, in the case of animals, suitability for sacrifice or human consumption. A list of clean and unclean animals is found in [11:1-47](Lev.11.1-Lev.11.47). The requirement for becoming clean after touching an unclean animal was merely to wash one’s clothes and remain apart from the community until evening ([11:25](Lev.11.25)). Most likely, therefore, the requirement of this sin offering indicates that the person had failed to follow the prescription for cleansing ([11:27-28](Lev.11.27-Lev.11.28)).

Any bodily discharge, even blood, would render a person temporarily **unclean** (chs [11–15](Lev.11.1-Lev.15.33)). The uncleanness itself was not sin, but it was a sin to neglect the uncleanness, allowing it to spread. Once people became aware of their unclean state, they were guilty if they neglected it.

Oaths could be taken in the name of the Lord. However, a **foolish vow,** one thoughtlessly made, was a blasphemous misuse of the Lord’s name ([Exod 20:7](Exod.20.7)). Accordingly, vows must be fulfilled (see [Num 30:2](Num.30.2); [Deut 23:21-23](Deut.23.21-Deut.23.23); [Eccl 5:4-6](Eccl.5.4-Eccl.5.6)).

**When you become aware of your guilt:** All the situations that required a sin offering assumed guilt by accident or ignorance. As soon as a person became aware of having done something improper, he or she became guilty and was required to attend to it. Known sins were to be dealt with; it was a sin in itself to know what was right and not do it (see [5:17](Lev.5.17); [Jas 4:17](Jas.4.17)).

**confess:** Sacrifice for sin without admission of guilt would be a meaningless ritual. When the sacrificial animal was presented to the priest, the worshiper likely told the priest why it was being offered.
The **penalty** was apparently fulfilled by the required sacrifice (see study note on 4:1–5:13).

The actions described in [5:1-5](Lev.5.1-Lev.5.5) best fit those of a layperson, so a **female** offering was permitted, in keeping with the principle demonstrated in [4:28](Lev.4.28), [32](Lev.4.32).

The poor also needed to secure atonement and reconciliation. Birds ([5:7](Lev.5.7)) were permitted for those too poor to afford a lamb (cp. [1:14-17](Lev.1.14-Lev.1.17)). Although an animal offering was typically required for atonement ([17:11](Lev.17.11)), God in his grace allowed the bloodless offering of flour if the worshiper could not even afford two birds ([5:11](Lev.5.11)).

The sin offerings included both a portion as a burnt offering and a portion that was first offered, then given to the priests (cp. [4:22-35](Lev.4.22-Lev.4.35); [6:24-30](Lev.6.24-Lev.6.30)). Because of their small size, two birds were required—one for each type of offering.

The sin offering was not to be adorned with **olive oil or . . . frankincense.** These were required for the grain offering, which was the individual’s gift to the Lord (see [2:1](Lev.2.1)), given to express worship. The sin offering made atonement; its purpose was to obtain forgiveness, requiring that the offering be completely unadorned.
**making them right:** See study notes on 1:4; 4:20.
**rest of the flour:** See study note on 2:3.

The **guilt offering** (Hebrew *’asham,* “guilt”) dealt with property loss and damages, whether sacred ([5:14-16](Lev.5.14-Lev.5.16)) or secular ([6:1-7](Lev.6.1-Lev.6.7)). It involved restitution as well as compensation for the loss ([5:16](Lev.5.16); [6:5](Lev.6.5)). It could be called a “penalty offering,” because the ram was a penalty, or perhaps a “restitution offering,” because of the need to make restitution for the loss before the ram was offered. In the guilt offering ([5:14–6:7](Lev.5.14-Lev.6.7)), the loss involved was not only a failure in God’s sight, as with the sin offering, but also a loss of property to another person or to the sanctuary. Cp. [Matt 5:23-24](Matt.5.23-Matt.5.24).

**unintentionally defiling:** Damage to sacred property was distinguished from damage to secular property. The sacrifice was effective only if the damage to sacred property had been committed accidentally. Deliberate damage, such as vandalism, to something sacred was blasphemous. As with other deliberate sins ([Num 15:30-31](Num.15.30-Num.15.31)), no means was specified for its atonement. No devout believer would defiantly continue in sin (see [1 Jn 3:9](1John.3.9)).

The **sanctuary shekel** was not a coin but a standardized unit for measuring weight. It was used to evaluate the ram being offered. Some scholars suggest that this text permits the substitution of the appropriate amount of silver for the ram.

The surcharge of **an additional 20 percent** provided compensation to the owner for loss or damage to property. The surcharge for sacred property was paid directly to the priests. Accidental damage to sacred property occurred when a person unintentionally ate the sacred offerings ([22:14](Lev.22.14)) or omitted the tithe ([27:31](Lev.27.31)). A similar surcharge was involved in redeeming an animal ([27:13](Lev.27.13), [27](Lev.27.27)).

This paragraph provides general principles for the guilt offering. Even if **unaware** of the infraction, an individual was **guilty** and had to provide the appropriate **guilt offering.** This applied to both sacred and secular property ([5:14-16](Lev.5.14-Lev.5.16); [6:1-7](Lev.6.1-Lev.6.7)).

**sins against your associate . . . unfaithful to the LORD:** For believers, there really is no such thing as a “secular” sin. All sin involves God, even sin directed against another person or group. In the sins requiring a guilt offering, God’s forgiveness was needed, but restitution to the injured individual had to be made first ([6:5-7](Lev.6.5-Lev.6.7); cp. [Matt 5:23-24](Matt.5.23-Matt.5.24)). Unlike offenses against sacred property ([Lev 5:14-16](Lev.5.14-Lev.5.16)), both accidental and intentional offenses against secular property could be forgiven.

The instructions for the guilt offering assumed that a person’s conscience would induce voluntary reparation; when restitution was voluntary, the surcharge for loss of use to the owner was always **20 percent.** Penalties were more severe in other cases (cp. [Exod 22:1-15](Exod.22.1-Exod.22.15)). There is a clear difference between voluntary confession and simply admitting sin after being caught.
**will purify you before the** **LORD, making you right with him:** God graciously gave his people a way to atone for their sins. See also study notes on 1:4; 4:20.

The regulations in [1:2–6:7](Lev.1.2-Lev.6.7) include instructions for both priest and layperson. This section adds detail regarding the rights and obligations of the officiating priest. Because the tribe of Levi had been allotted no land for farming ([Deut 18:1](Deut.18.1); [Josh 13:14](Josh.13.14), [33](Josh.13.33)), priests depended on the offering system for their income. The concern was that priests be adequately provided for. Like many human institutions, this system was eventually abused ([1 Sam 2:12-25](1Sam.2.12-1Sam.2.25); [Hos 4:8](Hos.4.8)).

The priest was required to wear **official linen clothing,** the attire of his office, when officiating at the Tabernacle. This allowed everyone to know that he was there to carry out his official duties ([Exod 28:40-43](Exod.28.40-Exod.28.43)). The priest was to dress appropriately for service to the divine King. He was not to wear his official garb outside the Tabernacle ([Lev 6:11](Lev.6.11); [Ezek 44:19](Ezek.44.19)).
**undergarments:** See [Exod 20:26](Exod.20.26).
Most natural environments qualified as a **place that is ceremonially clean.**

This passage cautions that **the fire on the** bronze **altar** must be constantly tended and **never** allowed to **go out***,* perhaps anticipating the tragedy of the “wrong kind of fire” offered by Nadab and Abihu ([10:1-2](Lev.10.1-Lev.10.2)).
In this context **sacred place** does not refer to the Holy Place at the heart of the Tabernacle but to any location within the Tabernacle complex, all of which were ceremonially clean and holy.
**yeast:** See study note on 2:11.

The priests’ **share** of the grain offering had the practical value of providing their staple food—bread ([7:9](Lev.7.9))—in addition to its theological significance as being **most holy.** See study note on 2:3.

The priestly share did not belong exclusively to the priest conducting the sacrifice; it was to be shared with all **of Aaron’s male descendants**. The text does not indicate why these offerings could be eaten only by the males while other offerings were available to all members of the priests’ families (see study note on 10:13-15; see also [Num 18:20-24](Num.18.20-Num.18.24)).

**will become holy:** Or *must be holy;* also in [Lev 6:27](Lev.6.27). Though uncleanness could be spread by touch (ch [15](Lev.15.1-Lev.15.33)), Haggai implied that holiness could not ([Hag 2:12](Hag.2.12)). If an unclean person encountered that which was holy, disaster could result ([Lev 10:1-3](Lev.10.1-Lev.10.3); [1 Sam 6:19-20](1Sam.6.19-1Sam.6.20); [2 Sam 6:6-8](2Sam.6.6-2Sam.6.8)).
These instructions applied only to the grain portion of the ordination offering (see [2:1-16](Lev.2.1-Lev.2.16); for the rest of the ordination offering, see [8:22-32](Lev.8.22-Lev.8.32)).
Only the **high priest** could represent the priesthood as an institution, with all its constituent priests.

Normally, the bulk of a grain offering would go to the officiating priest ([2:9-10](Lev.2.9-Lev.2.10)). However, the grain offering described in [6:19-23](Lev.6.19-Lev.6.23) was for a special occasion—the ordination of the priests—and therefore was to be **burned up entirely** and not **eaten.**

A **clay pot** was porous and could not be cleansed as thoroughly as a metal one—some of the holy food might stick to it or soak in. Reuse would cause an act of sacrilege. However, a **bronze pot** could be thoroughly **scoured** to prevent this problem (see also [11:33](Lev.11.33); [15:12](Lev.15.12)).

Some sin offerings for the anointed priest and for the entire congregation were not to be eaten. The blood of these offerings was carried into the Holy Place and sprinkled before the curtain (see [4:1-21](Lev.4.1-Lev.4.21)). The sacrifices that could be eaten were those for the lay leader and for the common people. The blood of these animals was poured on and around the base of the altar in the courtyard of the Tabernacle (see [4:22-35](Lev.4.22-Lev.4.35)).
The guilt offering required the sacrifice of a ram ([5:18](Lev.5.18)).

**fat . . . tail . . . organs:** The parts of the guilt offering to be burned were the same as those for the peace offering ([3:3-4](Lev.3.3-Lev.3.4), [9-10](Lev.3.9-Lev.3.10), [14-15](Lev.3.14-Lev.3.15)) and the sin offering ([4:8-9](Lev.4.8-Lev.4.9), [26](Lev.4.26), [31](Lev.4.31), [35](Lev.4.35)).

The **peace offering** could be presented as an expression of thanks (as here), as payment of a vow ([7:16](Lev.7.16)), or as a voluntary offering (see [3:1-7](Lev.3.1-Lev.3.7)). A worshiper made it an **expression of thanksgiving** by presenting a grain offering along with the peace offering ([2:1-16](Lev.2.1-Lev.2.16)). A grain offering consisted of unleavened cakes, wafers, or cakes of fine flour, all mixed or spread with olive oil. A representative portion was set aside to be burned ([2:9](Lev.2.9)). The grain offering was to be accompanied by loaves of yeast bread ([7:13](Lev.7.13)).

The **thanksgiving** offering was given when the worshiper was thankful ([Jer 17:26](Jer.17.26); [33:11](Jer.33.11)). The sacrifice was to be **eaten on the same day** it was offered so that the event would not fade from the worshiper’s memory.

In contrast to the “peace offering of thanksgiving,” which was presented as an expression of thanks to the Lord ([7:12-15](Lev.7.12-Lev.7.15)), the **offering to fulfill a vow** related to a vow made by a worshiper. The festive meal that followed was more relaxed and could extend into the next day. However, because the vow offering involved a vow made to God, it was still more restrictive than the voluntary offering, which could even use a deformed animal ([22:23](Lev.22.23)).

The Hebrew term for **contaminated** (*piggul*) occurs only in three other places ([19:7](Lev.19.7); [Isa 65:4](Isa.65.4); [Ezek 4:14](Ezek.4.14)). It is always used in reference to meat that is unacceptable for sacrifice or human consumption.

Anything that was **ceremonially unclean** could not come into contact with what was holy ([7:20](Lev.7.20)). Although uncleanness was not sinful in itself, it symbolized what was unholy (see [Exod 19:10](Exod.19.10)).

**cut off:** Three interpretations are possible for this expression, all of them very grave: (1) The person was subject to God’s judgment and faced an early death by natural causes ([17:10-14](Lev.17.10-Lev.17.14)). (2) The person was to be executed by the community (cp. [Exod 31:14](Exod.31.14)). (3) The person lost communal membership in Israel, either by banishment (such as by excommunication) or by shunning the person and treating him or her as unclean ([Lev 18:24-30](Lev.18.24-Lev.18.30); cp. [23:29-30](Lev.23.29-Lev.23.30), where “cut off” seems distinct from “destroy”).

In the sacrificial system, the **fat** and **blood** of all altar offerings belonged to God. They were offered before any of the sacrifice could be eaten. Consuming blood was specifically forbidden because it represented the very life of the animal ([17:10-16](Lev.17.10-Lev.17.16)). The injunction against eating fat might have been because fat, considered to be the best part of the offering, belonged to God.

Animals **found dead** had not been drained of their blood and were therefore unclean. Their fat was unfit to offer to the Lord and could not be eaten. However, it could be **used for any other purpose***,* such as greasing cart axles, waterproofing animal hides, and other household uses.
The prohibition against consuming blood was so important that the Council at Jerusalem included it in the instructions for Gentile believers ([Acts 15:29](Acts.15.29)).

**breast of the special offering . . . right thigh of the sacred offering:** The peace offering was a shared meal between God, the priest, the worshiper, and guests. The breast (in some older translations called a “wave offering”) and thigh (sometimes called the “contribution” or “heave offering”) were specifically designated as the priest’s portion (see [10:13-15](Lev.10.13-Lev.10.15)). After these offerings were taken into the Tabernacle and presented before the Lord, they could then be eaten (see [Exod 29:24](Exod.29.24), [26](Exod.29.26)).

In [Exod 28–29](Exod.28.1-Exod.29.46), the Lord gave Moses specific instructions for clothing and for ordaining Aaron and his sons as priests. In [Exod 39:1-31](Exod.39.1-Exod.39.31); [40:12-16](Exod.40.12-Exod.40.16); and [Lev 8](Lev.8.1-Lev.8.36), the commands were carried out. Moses didn’t just pass along the instructions verbally; he enacted the rituals to provide an example for the priests down to the last detail, **just as the** **LORD had commanded him** ([8:9](Lev.8.9), [13](Lev.8.13), [17](Lev.8.17), [21](Lev.8.21), [29](Lev.8.29)). Because the penalty for disobedience was death, God made sure the priests knew exactly what to do.
These items are also mentioned in [Exod 29:1-3](Exod.29.1-Exod.29.3), [7](Exod.29.7).
**sacred garments:** See [Exod 28](Exod.28.1-Exod.28.43).

The **anointing oil** consisted of special ingredients to give it a unique scent. These included myrrh, cinnamon, cane, and cassia (dried flowers from the cinnamon tree) mixed into olive oil (see [Exod 30:22-33](Exod.30.22-Exod.30.33)).
**bull for the sin offering:** See [Lev 4:3-12](Lev.4.3-Lev.4.12).
The first of the **two rams** was to be a whole burnt offering ([8:18](Lev.8.18)), while the second was a special ordination sacrifice ([8:22](Lev.8.22)).
**basket of bread made without yeast:** See [6:19-23](Lev.6.19-Lev.6.23).

The text repeatedly emphasizes that **Moses followed the** **LORD’s instructions,** obeying the commands given in [Exod 29](Exod.29.1-Exod.29.46) (see also [Lev 8:9](Lev.8.9), [13](Lev.8.13), [17](Lev.8.17), [21](Lev.8.21), [29](Lev.8.29), [36](Lev.8.36)).

Being **washed . . . with water** was the first step for cleansing from impurity. The priests had to be ceremonially clean before they could serve the Lord in holiness ([Exod 29:4](Exod.29.4); see [Ps 24:4](Ps.24.4)).
The **tunic** (see [Exod 28:39](Exod.28.39)) was woven of patterned linen cloth.

The same type of material used for the Tabernacle curtains was used for the embroidered **ephod** (see [Exod 28:4](Exod.28.4), [6-14](Exod.28.6-Exod.28.14)). This garment’s precise shape and size are unclear, but it seems to have been a long, sleeveless vest, fitted close to the body and tied about the waist. It was joined at the shoulders by gold settings; each setting bore an onyx stone engraved with the names of six of the tribes of Israel ([Exod 28:9](Exod.28.9)). Later, an ephod also referred to a venerated image ([Judg 8:27](Judg.8.27); [18:17](Judg.18.17)).
The **decorative sash** was embroidered and was made of the same materials as the ephod (see [Exod 28:8](Exod.28.8)).

The **chestpiece** (see [Exod 28:15-30](Exod.28.15-Exod.28.30)) was made of embroidered linen folded double. It bore twelve stones, each engraved with the name of a tribe of Israel. It was suspended over the heart by a gold chain from the gold shoulder-pieces of the ephod.

The **Urim and the Thummim** were placed in the pocket of the chestpiece ([Exod 28:30](Exod.28.30); [1 Sam 23:9-12](1Sam.23.9-1Sam.23.12); [30:7-8](1Sam.30.7-1Sam.30.8)); the precise function of these items is uncertain. They are generally thought of as two stones, perhaps each different in color, that were cast as lots. They apparently could give a positive, neutral, or negative answer to questions that could not otherwise be resolved ([Exod 28:30](Exod.28.30); [Num 27:21](Num.27.21); [1 Sam 28:6](1Sam.28.6)). Their mention in Old Testament prophetic literature written centuries later ([Ezra 2:63](Ezra.2.63); [Neh 7:65](Neh.7.65)) demonstrates how important these items were to the office of priest.

The **turban** worn by the high priest was made of linen and was distinct from the headdresses of the common priests ([Exod 28:40](Exod.28.40)). The **gold medallion** was suspended from the turban and bore an inscription that read, “Holy to the LORD” ([Exod 28:36](Exod.28.36)). With the names of the tribes on his shoulders and over his heart and the dedication to the Lord on his forehead, the high priest was clearly marked as the people’s representative to God and God’s representative to the people. In this mediating role, the high priest modeled the standard for all priests.

**making them holy:** God is the Holy One ([Pss 22:3](Ps.22.3); [78:41](Ps.78.41)). In the strictest sense, only God can make a person or thing holy ([Lev 20:8](Lev.20.8); [21:15](Lev.21.15), [23](Lev.21.23); [22:9](Lev.22.9), [16](Lev.22.16), [32](Lev.22.32); [Exod 31:13](Exod.31.13); see [Heb 2:11](Heb.2.11)); the actions of Moses simply recognized and declared what God had done (also in [Lev 8:11](Lev.8.11), [12](Lev.8.12), [15](Lev.8.15)).
For the attire of the common priests, see [Exod 28:40-41](Exod.28.40-Exod.28.41).
**sin offering** (see [4:3-12](Lev.4.3-Lev.4.12)): Two atoning offerings were made—the sin offering ([8:14-17](Lev.8.14-Lev.8.17)) and the whole burnt offering ([8:18-21](Lev.8.18-Lev.8.21)).
By placing **their hands on the bull’s head** (see [1:4](Lev.1.4)), Aaron and his sons were identifying themselves with the sacrifice (also in [8:18](Lev.8.18), [22](Lev.8.22)).

Normally, the high priest performed these priestly duties. However, it would not be proper for the priests to ordain themselves, so **Moses,** acting as God’s representative, instituted the priesthood.
**ram for the burnt offering:** See study note on 1:10-13.
**ram of ordination:** See [Exod 29:19-34](Exod.29.19-Exod.29.34).

Aaron’s **\[ear\]lobe, thumb,** and **big toe** represented his total person. This act emphasized the role of the priestly office, with the blood stressing the ties to the sacrificial system. The priest’s basic function was mediation between God and his people. To do this effectively, he needed ears that could hear the words of God and the needs of his people, hands ready to do God’s bidding, and feet ready to take him where he was needed.
Moses functioned as a priest in the ordination ceremony and so received the priest’s **portion** of the offering (see [8:15](Lev.8.15)).
**anointing oil:** See study note on 8:2; see also [Ps 133:2](Ps.133.2).

The ordination offering was a variation of the peace offering ([Exod 29:28](Exod.29.28)). It was a meal ([Lev 7:11-18](Lev.7.11-Lev.7.18), [28-34](Lev.7.28-Lev.7.34)) shared between God (the parts burned on the altar) and the priests. The command to **boil . . . and eat** the ordination offering first appears in [Exod 29:32](Exod.29.32).

**commanded by the** **LORD:** The details of the sacrifice rituals were symbolic and important in their own right. Yet most important, the priests were to obey God’s commands. Complete obedience to God is a major theme in both the Old Testament and the New Testament: “Obedience is better than sacrifice” ([1 Sam 15:22](1Sam.15.22)).

**seven days:** This command emphasized God’s absolute holiness and mandated strict compliance with his commands. The priests, now anointed as God’s holy servants, were to remain in the Tabernacle court for **seven days** before venturing out into everyday life.
**eighth day:** The priests had finished the seven-day period of probation commanded in [8:35](Lev.8.35).
**elders:** See study note on 4:15.

These sacrifices—the sin and whole burnt offerings for the priests and the sin, burnt, peace, and grain offerings for the people—were offered at the beginning of the priests’ ministry to make certain that all sin was atoned for and the covenant with God affirmed. Only the guilt offering was omitted.

Just as *holiness* describes God’s person and nature, the **glory of the** **LORD** tangibly expresses his power and majesty (see [Ezek 1:28](Ezek.1.28); [10:4](Ezek.10.4)). His glory was revealed on Mount Sinai ([Exod 24:16](Exod.24.16)), at the dedication of the Tabernacle ([Exod 40:34-35](Exod.40.34-Exod.40.35)), and in Solomon’s Temple ([1 Kgs 8:11](1Kgs.8.11); [2 Chr 7:1](2Chr.7.1)). Yet it remained as vast as the heavens ([Ps 19:1](Ps.19.1)). The New Testament speaks of Christ’s glory as the image of God ([2 Cor 4:4](2Cor.4.4)), who manifested God’s glory to the world ([John 1:14](John.1.14)). He was glorified in his death and resurrection ([John 17:1-5](John.17.1-John.17.5)). See also [Exod 24:15-17](Exod.24.15-Exod.24.17).
**your sin offering . . . burnt offering:** Before the high priest could make atonement for the people, he had to be right with God himself.

Both Aaron, the high priest ([9:8](Lev.9.8), [12](Lev.9.12)), and **his sons,** the common priests ([9:9](Lev.9.9), [12](Lev.9.12), [13](Lev.9.13)), participated in the sin offering ([9:8-11](Lev.9.8-Lev.9.11)) and the burnt offering ([9:12-14](Lev.9.12-Lev.9.14)). This made the atonement effective for the entire priesthood.
**horns of the altar:** See study note on 4:25; see also [Exod 27:1-8](Exod.27.1-Exod.27.8).
**regular burnt offering for the morning:** A lamb was offered as a whole burnt offering each morning and evening ([6:9](Lev.6.9); [Num 28:2-4](Num.28.2-Num.28.4)).
**blessed them:** See [Num 6:22-27](Num.6.22-Num.6.27).
**Fire blazed forth from the** **LORD’s presence,** indicating that God had accepted the offerings, the atonement, and the priesthood ([9:7](Lev.9.7); cp. [1 Kgs 18:36-38](1Kgs.18.36-1Kgs.18.38)).

A fire was to burn constantly on the bronze altar ([6:9](Lev.6.9)) to supply coals for burning incense ([16:12](Lev.16.12)). Perhaps careless from drinking wine ([10:8-11](Lev.10.8-Lev.10.11)), Nadab and Abihu took coals from another source. This violation of God’s instruction resulted in their deaths.

Aaron’s two older sons, **Nadab and Abihu** ([Exod 6:23](Exod.6.23)), had accompanied Moses and the seventy elders on Mount Sinai ([Exod 24:1](Exod.24.1), [9](Exod.24.9)) and had witnessed the great theophany (appearance of God) there. They died without male heirs (see also [Exod 28:1](Exod.28.1); [Num 3:2-4](Num.3.2-Num.3.4); [26:60-61](Num.26.60-Num.26.61); [1 Chr 6:3](1Chr.6.3); [24:1-2](1Chr.24.1-1Chr.24.2)).

The **incense burners** were fire pans or trays that held hot coals. Incense was sprinkled on them ([Exod 30:34-38](Exod.30.34-Exod.30.38); see also [Lev 16:12-13](Lev.16.12-Lev.16.13); [2 Chr 26:19](2Chr.26.19); [Rev 8:3-4](Rev.8.3-Rev.8.4)).

The **wrong kind of fire** (Hebrew *’esh zarah,* “strange fire”) could mean “foreign,” and thus “unauthorized” (see [Exod 30:9](Exod.30.9)) or even “pagan” (as in [Ps 44:20](Ps.44.20); [81:9](Ps.81.9)). Apparently, Nadab and Abihu used fire from a source not approved by God ([Num 3:4](Num.3.4); [26:61](Num.26.61)), possibly even a pagan source. It is also possible that they offered incense not prepared according to God’s specifications ([Exod 30:34-38](Exod.30.34-Exod.30.38)), although the text does not mention that. They did not enter God’s presence on his terms but on their own.

In [9:24](Lev.9.24), the **fire blazed forth** to show God’s acceptance. It now indicates his disapproval by bringing death to Nadab and Abihu, who had demonstrated a careless approach toward the worship of God (cp. [Acts 5:1-11](Acts.5.1-Acts.5.11)).

God’s **holiness** is his very essence, substance, and character, and it stands in contrast to the creaturely world. By performing this rash act, Nadab and Abihu failed to consider God’s holiness and failed to honor him.
**Mishael and Elzaphan . . . uncle Uzziel:** See [Exod 6:18](Exod.6.18), [22](Exod.6.22).

**carry away the bodies of your relatives:** Aaron, the high priest, and the priests Eleazar and Ithamar ([Lev 10:6](Lev.10.6)) could not defile themselves by making contact with a dead person ([21:10-12](Lev.21.10-Lev.21.12)).
Carrying the bodies **by their garments** avoided defilement.
**Eleazar and Ithamar** were Aaron’s two remaining sons ([Exod 6:23](Exod.6.23)).

**leaving your hair uncombed:** This practice and others like it were ways to **show grief** in biblical times (cp. [Gen 37:29](Gen.37.29); [44:13](Gen.44.13); [Deut 14:1](Deut.14.1); [2 Sam 1:11](2Sam.1.11); [Job 1:20](Job.1.20); [Jer 16:6](Jer.16.6); [47:5](Jer.47.5)). As high priest, Aaron was prohibited from participating in these rituals or in any way displaying his grief ([Lev 21:10](Lev.21.10)). The injunction extended to **Eleazar and Ithamar***;* if God’s representatives had shown grief on this occasion, it might have been interpreted by observers as disagreeing with God’s justice. However, the laypeople were allowed to mourn.
**must not leave:** Eleazar and Ithamar were not to attend the funeral.
**the** **LORD’s anointing oil:** Because they had recently been **anointed** as priests (see [7:36](Lev.7.36)), they were to avoid any association with the dead.

The placement of this instruction suggests that Nadab and Abihu were under the influence of alcohol when they offered “the wrong kind of fire” ([10:1](Lev.10.1)). Priests were not to drink anything that could impair their judgment before serving in the Tabernacle.
**the** **LORD said to Aaron:** God had been communicating only to Moses, but he now accepted Aaron as the people’s representative, and he communicated directly with Aaron as well.
The word **common** means “secular” or “ordinary.”
**ceremonially unclean . . . clean:** See [7:19-21](Lev.7.19-Lev.7.21); [11:1–15:33](Lev.11.1-Lev.15.33).
The **decrees that the** **LORD has given** were laws that came directly from God, rather than from a court decision.
The **grain offering** was part of the ordination ceremony (see [8:26](Lev.8.26); [Exod 29:2](Exod.29.2), [23](Exod.29.23)).

**no yeast, for it is most holy:** Realizing that some time had passed, Moses wanted to be certain that no fermentation had occurred in the priest’s portion of the grain offering ([Lev 6:14-18](Lev.6.14-Lev.6.18)).

The priest’s share of the grain offering, the sin offering, and the guilt offering was “most holy” (see [2:3](Lev.2.3); [6:29](Lev.6.29); [7:6](Lev.7.6)). Only the males in the priest’s family could eat it, and it had to be consumed in a holy place (that is, the Tabernacle court). The priest’s portion of the peace offering, though, was considered simply “holy.” It could be eaten by any family member in any clean place ([22:10-13](Lev.22.10-Lev.22.13)).

**The goat of the sin offering** was the offering for the people ([9:3](Lev.9.3), [15-17](Lev.9.15-Lev.9.17); cp. [9:2](Lev.9.2), [8-11](Lev.9.8-Lev.9.11)). On this special occasion, its blood was not carried into the Holy Place as required. The remaining portion, after the portions allocated to God had been offered, should have been eaten by the priests (see [6:29](Lev.6.29)). But the goat was entirely burned, even though its blood had not been taken into the sanctuary ([10:18](Lev.10.18); see [6:30](Lev.6.30)).

**yet this tragedy has happened to me:** Aaron was saying either that eating the goat of the sin offering would not have prevented the deaths of Nadab and Abihu or that it would not have been appropriate for him to eat it on the heels of such a grievous event.

These chapters detail the regulations pertaining to purity. The mixing of types of animals was forbidden (see [Deut 22:9-11](Deut.22.9-Deut.22.11)) because it represented a violation of the normal created order. “Abnormal” creatures—such as fish without fins and scales, carnivores, crawling insects, and animals without split hooves—cross boundaries between “normal” types and were unfit for food or offerings (see also [Deut 14:1-21](Deut.14.1-Deut.14.21)). The dietary laws were meant to distinguish Israel as a holy people from the surrounding nations ([Lev 11:44-45](Lev.11.44-Lev.11.45)).

Some scholars have suggested that unclean animals were to be avoided for reasons of public health, but the evidence does not support this. Horse meat, for example, is no less healthy than beef, yet it was considered unclean because the horse does not have a split hoof (see [11:2-3](Lev.11.2-Lev.11.3)). The regulations existed because an unclean animal was unacceptable as an offering to God and, therefore, it was also unacceptable as food for God’s people. Jesus proclaimed all foods clean for Christians ([Mark 7:14-19](Mark.7.14-Mark.7.19); [Acts 10:9-16](Acts.10.9-Acts.10.16)).
**these . . . you may use for food:** Animals that have **split hooves** and chew the **cud** were considered “normal” and ceremonially clean (see also [Deut 14:3-21](Deut.14.3-Deut.14.21)).
Neither the **hyrax** nor the **hare** truly chews the cud, though both appear to. They are considered unclean because they do not have split hooves.
**marine animals:** Fish considered clean for the Israelites had both **fins and scales**.
The prohibition included fish such as eels and sharks that have **fins** but not **scales,** as well as crustaceans and mollusks, which have neither fins nor scales.

The list of unclean **birds** includes birds of prey and scavengers, both of which come in contact with dead animals and blood. This renders them unclean and unfit. Bats ([11:19](Lev.11.19)) fly, but are not birds; they are therefore “abnormal” and ceremonially unclean.

**insects that walk along the ground and have jointed legs:** This phrase eliminates creatures that creep or crawl low to the ground ([11:27](Lev.11.27)). [Leviticus 11:42](Lev.11.42) indicates that multi-legged creatures, such as centipedes, are unclean. **Locusts** and **grasshoppers** are examples of clean insects (see [Matt 3:4](Matt.3.4)).
**defiled until evening:** Anyone who touched a carcass of an unclean animal would be unclean until evening, which marked the beginning of the next day in Israel.
This list of unclean creatures that crawl contains both warm-blooded and cold-blooded animals that scurry along the ground. Snakes are also included in this category ([11:42](Lev.11.42)).

Dead animals could make things and people unclean. Even a clean animal that died without having its blood drained was considered unclean ([11:39-40](Lev.11.39-Lev.11.40)). When a person became unclean from contact with an animal’s carcass, it lasted only until evening. Household articles that came into contact with a carcass had to be purified ([11:25](Lev.11.25), [28](Lev.11.28), [32](Lev.11.32), [40](Lev.11.40)) or destroyed ([11:33](Lev.11.33), [35](Lev.11.35)).
A **cistern** was a hole dug into the ground or rock, often lined with plaster, that retained rain and surface water.

**Grain** moistened with water was probably intended to be cooked for food; eating contaminated grain would be like eating a carcass. However, if the grain was sown, the new plant and the grain it bore were undefiled.

Israelites were not to consume blood ([7:26](Lev.7.26)). They could eat an animal only after the blood had been drained and properly disposed of ([17:13](Lev.17.13)). The undrained blood of an otherwise clean animal that died of natural causes rendered it unclean. An Israelite was permitted to give or sell such an animal to foreigners ([Deut 14:21](Deut.14.21)) but not to eat it.
**I am the** **LORD your God:** See study note on 18:2.

**be holy, because I am holy:** These words express the dominant theme of Leviticus: God is holy. He must be regarded and treated as holy, and he expects holiness from his people ([10:3](Lev.10.3); [19:2](Lev.19.2)). The profound teaching of this verse is that God’s own nature permeates those who covenant with him (see also [11:45](Lev.11.45); [20:7](Lev.20.7), [26](Lev.20.26); [21:8](Lev.21.8), [15](Lev.21.15); [22:9](Lev.22.9), [16](Lev.22.16), [32](Lev.22.32)), and they become his holy people ([Exod 22:31](Exod.22.31); [Deut 28:9](Deut.28.9); cp. [1 Pet 1:16](1Pet.1.16)).

**brought you up from the land of Egypt:** This or a similar phrase is found often throughout the Pentateuch (see [19:36](Lev.19.36); [22:33](Lev.22.33); [25:38](Lev.25.38); [26:13](Lev.26.13); [Exod 13:9](Exod.13.9); [20:2](Exod.20.2); [Num 15:41](Num.15.41); [Deut 4:37](Deut.4.37)). Each time, it reminds the Israelites, God’s covenant people, of God’s great act in liberating them from Egypt. The Exodus event is frequently commemorated elsewhere in the Old Testament ([Pss 80:8](Ps.80.8); [106:21](Ps.106.21); [Isa 11:16](Isa.11.16); [Jer 34:13](Jer.34.13); [Hos 12:9](Hos.12.9); [13:4](Hos.13.4); [Amos 2:10](Amos.2.10)).

These verses detail the regulations pertaining to childbirth. Any bodily discharge, even blood, was considered “abnormal” because it reduced the vitality of the individual and rendered the person ceremonially unclean (see study notes on 5:3; 11:1–15:33). Accordingly, not childbirth but the discharge accompanying it is addressed in these verses ([12:2](Lev.12.2), [5](Lev.12.5), [7](Lev.12.7)). The uncleanness was not sinful in itself, but only if it was neglected and allowed to come into contact with what is holy (see [5:2-3](Lev.5.2-Lev.5.3)).
**menstrual period:** See [15:19-24](Lev.15.19-Lev.15.24).
By the **eighth day***,* a baby’s system has developed to a point where the blood can clot properly, rendering circumcision relatively safe.
These **thirty-three days** are added to the seven previous days ([12:2](Lev.12.2), [3](Lev.12.3)) to yield a total of forty days to complete the mother’s period of purification.
**two weeks . . . sixty-six days:** The total is eighty days, double the time required for the birth of a son (see also [27:2-7](Lev.27.2-Lev.27.7)).

**purification offering:** The Hebrew word is the same as that for the sin offering (*khatta’t,* see study note on 4:1–5:13). This leads some scholars to think that this offering dealt only with purification or decontamination, including those cases mentioned in [5:1-6](Lev.5.1-Lev.5.6). The offering here was certainly part of a purification ritual, but it seems more likely that the sin offering repaired a lack or failure. In this context, the issue is purity rather than sin, and the focus is on restoring the woman to community fellowship, not forgiving a sinner.
**to purify her:** “Atonement” can be understood in this context to stress ceremonial cleansing and reconciliation of the worshiper (see [4:20](Lev.4.20); see also study note on 1:4).
**cannot afford to bring a lamb:** The alternative offering provided for the poorer class of society (see [5:7-13](Lev.5.7-Lev.5.13); cp. [Luke 2:22-24](Luke.2.22-Luke.2.24)).

Concerning the regulations pertaining to infections, the principle of normal and abnormal comes into play (see “Clean, Unclean, and Holy” Theme Note). Whether in a person, clothing, or a building, infections are not normal: They indicate disease and death, the antitheses of wholeness, and were therefore declared unclean.

**a serious skin disease** (Hebrew *tsara‘at*): The Hebrew word is much broader than the severely disfiguring Hansen’s disease (see study note on 13:2). This larger range included symptoms such as an open sore ([13:10](Lev.13.10)), a boil ([13:18](Lev.13.18)), a burn ([13:24](Lev.13.24)), a sore on the head or chin ([13:29](Lev.13.29)), shiny white patches ([13:38](Lev.13.38)), or abnormal baldness ([13:40](Lev.13.40)). A general test was whether or not the abnormality was spreading ([13:5-8](Lev.13.5-Lev.13.8)). If so, a quarantine was ordered for as long as the disorder persisted ([13:46](Lev.13.46)). Not just people, but clothing ([13:47-59](Lev.13.47-Lev.13.59)) and even buildings ([14:33-53](Lev.14.33-Lev.14.53)) could contract such infections.

Skin disorders that were potentially contagious, such as **swelling or a rash or discolored skin,** required precautions to arrest their spread. Until a disorder was healed, the person was deemed unclean. The diseases described in this section may range from something as simple as an allergic rash, ringworm, or eczema to something as serious as gangrene. In Old Testament times, skin conditions were diagnosed by observation. The priests not only had a religious function, but they also served as physicians.
**one of his sons:** These priestly functions were to apply to future generations of priests as well.

**more than skin-deep:** This indicates that either the infection had eaten away the skin or the infection was visible beneath the skin. The white hair, together with the depression in the skin, indicated a skin disease that could spread ([13:21-23](Lev.13.21-Lev.13.23)). This made the person unclean ([13:8](Lev.13.8)).
The purpose of a **quarantine** was primarily diagnostic. It gave the priest an opportunity to examine the patient’s symptoms over a period of time.
If **the rash** had **spread,** then the priest declared the person unclean and the isolation became long-term.
The presence of an **open sore** was the crucial factor, because it indicated infection.

The **completely white** skin might refer simply to a loss of pigment (see also [13:3](Lev.13.3)), whereas raw flesh ([13:10](Lev.13.10), [14](Lev.13.14)) indicated infection and ceremonial uncleanness.
The priest was to inspect the **burned area** to see if the wound had become infected (see [13:9-17](Lev.13.9-Lev.13.17)).
**hair . . . turned white:** See [13:18-23](Lev.13.18-Lev.13.23).
The **scabby sore** suggested a fungal infection in the scalp or beard, hidden by hair. The symptoms included loss of hair and crusty skin.

If a **skin rash** showed pus or inflammation ([13:42](Lev.13.42)), it was probably an infection. If it only showed as a whitened area, it was probably vitiligo (leucoderma). With this harmless disorder, patches of skin lose their pigmentation.
A **reddish white sore** perhaps indicated pus and inflammation.
Tearing one’s **clothing,** letting one’s hair go **uncombed,** and covering the **mouth** were common ways of expressing mourning ([10:6](Lev.10.6)).

The cry of **Unclean! Unclean!** denoted social unacceptability as much as a health threat. It warned others that the individual’s skin disorder could be contagious and that holy things should not touch the unclean person.

The Tabernacle containing the Ark was in the center of the camp so that God could be considered as being in the camp ([Deut 23:14](Deut.23.14)). As long as an individual’s skin disorder persisted, he or she was to stay **in isolation . . . outside the camp.** This ensured that the infection would not spread to others and that the uncleanness would not come in contact with holy things. Even Miriam, sister of Moses and Aaron, had to spend seven days outside the camp ([Num 12:15](Num.12.15)). This area was not exclusive to those suffering from skin disorders. The uneaten sin offering was taken there and burned ([Lev 4:21](Lev.4.21)). Criminals were executed there ([24:14](Lev.24.14), [23](Lev.24.23)), and corpses were carried there to avoid contaminating the area where the people lived ([10:4-5](Lev.10.4-Lev.10.5)). Even bodily functions were attended to outside the camp ([Deut 23:12-14](Deut.23.12-Deut.23.14)).

The rainy season in Israel, when the weather is humid and cool, extends from mid-October through March. Mildew flourishes during this time, and the spores can trigger serious allergic reactions, posing a health problem. The regulations for mildew in clothing were similar to those for infections in people. If the mildew showed signs of spreading, it was serious. If it could be stopped or washed or cut out, a garment could be saved. This process was also similar to the treatment of rot and mold in buildings ([14:33-53](Lev.14.33-Lev.14.53)).
**mildew:** The word refers here to a variety of molds or mildews that infected cloth or leather.
These verses, dealing with the purification of infected individuals, are best understood when read in conjunction with [13:1-46](Lev.13.1-Lev.13.46).

The items listed here were part of the cleansing ritual involving the ashes of the red heifer ([Num 19:6](Num.19.6)), but their exact significance is unknown. See also [Heb 9:18-22](Heb.9.18-Heb.9.22). **Hyssop** was a small plant used for sprinkling blood ([Exod 12:22](Exod.12.22)) and in purification rites ([Num 19:18](Num.19.18)).

Killing the bird and sprinkling its blood ([14:7](Lev.14.7)) reflects [Exod 24:6-8](Exod.24.6-Exod.24.8), where all of Israel was sprinkled with blood to establish the people as God’s covenant community. Here the individual was cleansed by being sprinkled with blood and allowed to return to community membership. Fresh water was also used in cleansing ceremonies ([Num 8:7](Num.8.7)) and in sacrifice preparation ([Lev 1:9](Lev.1.9), [13](Lev.1.13)).

Just as the goat released to Azazel symbolized the removal of sin from the community on the Day of Atonement ([16:10](Lev.16.10), [20-22](Lev.16.20-Lev.16.22)), the **release** of **the live bird** symbolized the removal of the individual’s uncleanness.

This **guilt offering** (sometimes called the “penalty offering” or “reparation offering”) was offered because the unclean person living outside the camp could not bring sacrifices, tithes, and offerings during the period of uncleanness (see [5:14-16](Lev.5.14-Lev.5.16)).
The **lobe, thumb,** and **big toe** represent what the whole person hears and does, and where he or she goes (also [14:17](Lev.14.17), [28](Lev.14.28); see study note on 8:23).

In the ancient world, **olive oil** was commonly used to aid healing (see [Isa 1:6](Isa.1.6); [Luke 10:34](Luke.10.34)). Its use here might symbolize the healing and cleansing of the infection, which allowed the person to return to the community. Perhaps it also represented restored union between God, the priest, and the worshiper.
This **sin offering** was the offering of purification mentioned in [12:6](Lev.12.6) (see [4:2-3](Lev.4.2-Lev.4.3)).
The **burnt offering** provided atonement for sins committed during the period of uncleanness when the person was unable to bring offerings (see [1:4](Lev.1.4)).
**grain offering:** See study note on 2:1-16.
The ritual for the **poor** was very similar to the conventional purification offering, but it allowed for the use of less expensive birds in place of a lamb (see [5:7-13](Lev.5.7-Lev.5.13)).

The contamination of buildings by rot or mildew made them unhealthy or even unsafe. These buildings were considered diseased and therefore not whole or clean (see study note on 11:1–15:33). The inspection and treatment process was similar to the one for mildew in clothing ([13:47-59](Lev.13.47-Lev.13.59)).

**I may contaminate:** In the absolute monotheism of biblical language, God causes or allows everything. For example, [Exod 21:13](Exod.21.13) describes an accidental death as something that God allowed to happen (see also [Deut 19:4-5](Deut.19.4-Deut.19.5)).
Having **the house emptied** indicated that it was not actually unclean until the priest pronounced it so. The owner would remove furnishings so that they would not be included in the quarantine.

If the mildew extended **deeper than the wall’s surface** it was more serious than if it were just on the surface. The same idea was expressed by “more than skin-deep” in the examination of infected individuals (see study note on 13:3).
A summary statement about infections of all sorts (cp. [11:46-47](Lev.11.46-Lev.11.47)).

The principle of normal and abnormal and the created order again aids the interpretation of these regulations (see “Clean, Unclean, and Holy” Theme Note). Bodily discharges, such as infections (see study note on 13:1-46), were not “normal” because they weakened the vitality of the person, so the person was not seen as whole. Whether male ([15:1-18](Lev.15.1-Lev.15.18)) or female ([15:19-33](Lev.15.19-Lev.15.33)), such a person became unclean.

**bodily discharge** (literally *a flowing from his flesh*): Most scholars interpret the word *flesh* as a euphemism for sexual organs and the symptoms described here as indicating an infection of gonorrhea. Others suggest that it refers to a discharge of semen or even diarrhea. A discharge of semen is unlikely, however, because that is singled out in [15:16-17](Lev.15.16-Lev.15.17) and required only washing with water. It is clear that this bodily discharge proceeded from “under the man” ([15:10](Lev.15.10)) and contaminated anything he sat on or lay upon ([15:4](Lev.15.4), [6](Lev.15.6), [9](Lev.15.9)).

In contrast to the man with a skin disease (see [13:46](Lev.13.46)), a man with a bodily discharge was apparently allowed to live at home. He did not have to undergo the more elaborate cleansing ritual described in ch [14](Lev.14.1-Lev.14.57). He simply had to wait seven days after the discharge ceased, wash ([15:13](Lev.15.13)), and present the least expensive animal sacrifice of two birds—one as a **sin offering** and the other as a whole **burnt offering.**

In the case of an **emission of semen***,* the discharge was not a sign of illness (see study note on 15:1-33). Still, the same rule applied; the man must wash and be considered unclean until the next evening.

If the seminal emission involved **sexual intercourse***,* both the man and the woman became unclean and had to wash and remain unclean until the next evening. Although it involved a bodily emission, sexual intercourse was not an infection or abnormality, and it required no sacrifices.

There is nothing wrong or diseased about a woman’s **menstrual period**.
